html:
In 1648 French and Dutch settlers agreed to divide the island of Saint Martin between them in the Treaty of Concordia. The north became French and the south Dutch.

A popular legend says the line was set by a walk: a Frenchman and a Dutchman set off round the coast, and the Frenchman went further. The real reasons were the salt ponds, which the Dutch West India Company wanted, and the wars with Spain.

The border changed a few times in the wars that followed but settled in 1817. It is one of the oldest open borders in the world. The south is today Sint Maarten in the Kingdom of the Netherlands; the north is a French collectivity.
sum: In 1648 French and Dutch settlers agreed to divide the island of Saint Martin between them in the Treaty of Concordia. The north became French and the south Dutch.
